title: How a torn QR code still works

segments.text: How does a QR code still work when it's torn?
A whole corner is gone, and your camera still reads it.
Step one: the three big squares tell your camera where the code is, and which way up it is, from any angle.
Step two: each small square is a one or a zero.
And next to your message, the code stores extra repair data.
Step three, the clever part: like a sudoku puzzle, the missing pieces can be worked out from the ones that are left.
On the strongest setting, up to about thirty percent of the data can be rebuilt.
That's why some codes have a logo in the middle.
But if you cover one of the three big squares, many scanners can't even find the code.

sources: https://www.denso-wave.com/en/system/qr/fundamental/qrcode/qrc/index.html (Denso Wave, inventor: 'Since QR Code has an error correction function, data can be recovered even in parts of the code that are stained or damaged.')
https://www.qrcode.com/en/history/ (Denso Wave: position detection pattern with 1:1:3:1:1 ratio; orientation detected 'regardless of the angle of scanning, which could be any angle out of 360°')
ISO/IEC 18004 Reed-Solomon block tables, as implemented in the python-qrcode library: at level H, half the repair codewords = 30.8-33.2% of all codewords across versions 1-40
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_code (secondary: levels L/M/Q/H restore approx. 7/15/25/30% of codewords; Reed-Solomon error correction)

Own decode tests (qr_tests.py, qa_scan.py; OpenCV + ZXing): level H on a dark background scans with 13-18% of its area torn from a corner (video uses ~15%), fails at 20%; level L fails at every tested tear size; covering any one of the three finder squares makes both decoders fail. Every rendered frame was checked.
